title: Autocovariance of AR Processes
breadcrumb: Time series → Foundations → Computing γₖ from the coefficients
engineName: Time series — multiply through, take expectations, and solve
objectives: Derive the AR(1) variance and autocorrelation function from the model equation.
State and apply γ₀ = σ²/(1 − φ²) and ρₖ = φᵏ.
Derive ρ₁ = φ₁/(1 − φ₂) for an AR(2) using the symmetry γ₋ₖ = γₖ.
Run the recursion ρₖ = φ₁ρₖ₋₁ + φ₂ρₖ₋₂ from its two starting values.
Use the closed-form AR(2) variance and read its sign as a stationarity check.
Say why only the k = 0 equation carries σ² and why autocorrelations do not.

prereq.name: Weak stationarity
prereq.why: It is what makes E(yₜyₜ₋ₖ) depend on k alone, turning the calculation into a recursion.

prereq.name: White noise and its properties
prereq.why: E(yₜ₋ₖεₜ) = 0 for k ≥ 1 is what kills the cross terms; E(yₜεₜ) = σ² is what survives at k = 0.

prereq.name: Stationarity conditions (topic 7.1)
prereq.why: The formulas are valid only inside the admissible region, and the variance's sign reports when they are not.

prereq.name: Linear difference equations
prereq.why: The autocorrelations satisfy one, and its root structure explains smooth versus oscillating decay.

traps: ρ₁ = φ₁ holds for an AR(1) only; for an AR(2) it is φ₁/(1 − φ₂).
Only the k = 0 equation carries σ² — the recursion for k ≥ 1 is homogeneous.
E(yₜεₜ) = σ², not zero. Forgetting it loses the variance entirely.
The variance depends on φ², so its value is the same at φ and −φ.
Autocorrelations never involve σ²; the variance always does.
An oscillating ACF means complex roots, not an MA component.
γ₋₁ = γ₁ by symmetry — the AR(2) derivation fails without it.
A negative variance from the formula means the coefficients are outside the triangle.

sheet: METHOD: multiply the model by yₜ₋ₖ, take expectations, use stationarity to get a recursion in k.
E(yₜ₋ₖεₜ) = 0 for k ≥ 1; E(yₜεₜ) = σ². Only the k = 0 equation carries σ².
AR(1) recursion: γₖ = φγₖ₋₁, so γₖ = φᵏγ₀ and ρₖ = φᵏ.
AR(1) variance: γ₀ = φγ₁ + σ² = φ²γ₀ + σ² ⟹ γ₀ = σ²/(1 − φ²).
The variance depends on φ², so it is the same at φ = ±0.7. Sign changes the SHAPE only.
AR(2) recursion: γₖ = φ₁γₖ₋₁ + φ₂γₖ₋₂ (k ≥ 1), and the same in ρ.
At k = 1: ρ₁ = φ₁ + φ₂ρ₋₁ = φ₁ + φ₂ρ₁ (using ρ₋₁ = ρ₁) ⟹ ρ₁ = φ₁/(1 − φ₂).
Then ρ₂ = φ₁ρ₁ + φ₂, and the recursion onwards. At (0.5,0.3): 0.7143, 0.6571, 0.5429, 0.3971.
Simulated at (0.5,0.3): 0.7145, 0.6577, 0.5432, 0.3975 — agreement to three decimals.
AR(2) VARIANCE: γ₀ = σ²(1 − φ₂)/[(1 + φ₂)((1 − φ₂)² − φ₁²)].
The denominator factors (1+φ₂)(1−φ₂−φ₁)(1−φ₂+φ₁) — the three stationarity conditions.
So γ₀ > 0 ⟺ the process is stationary. A negative value is a diagnosis, not an error.
The recursion is a difference equation with characteristic equation z² − φ₁z − φ₂ = 0.
Distinct real roots → ρₖ = Az₁ᵏ + Bz₂ᵏ; repeated → (A + Bk)zᵏ; complex → Crᵏ sin(ωk + δ).
Complex roots when φ₁² + 4φ₂ < 0, with damping r = √|φ₂| — reciprocal of topic 7.1's 1/√|φ₂|.
The recursion is homogeneous, so it fixes the SHAPE; the k = 0 equation fixes the SCALE.
Effective sample size for a persistent AR(1): about n(1−φ)/(1+φ) — only ~10 at n = 200, φ = 0.9.
tricks: Check the three stationarity conditions BEFORE substituting into any formula.
For an AR(1), ρ₁ is the coefficient; for an AR(2) it is not — divide by (1 − φ₂).
A negative φ₂ ENLARGES 1 − φ₂, so it reduces ρ₁ relative to φ₁.
Any AR variance must exceed σ². A value below it means an error somewhere.
ρ₂ = φ₁ρ₁ + φ₂ is quicker than restarting the recursion from scratch.
At φ₂ = 0 every AR(2) formula must collapse to the AR(1) one — a free check.
remember: ρ₁ = φ₁/(1 − φ₂) for an AR(2).
A negative variance means non-stationary coefficients.

howto: Section 3 contains the method and all four formulas, and section 4 then does the AR(2) calculation from first principles with a simulation as a check — those two sections together are the lesson. The single device to internalise is in section 3's first block: multiply by yₜ₋ₖ, take expectations, and let stationarity turn the result into a recursion. Two things make that calculation go wrong, and both are flagged repeatedly: the symmetry γ₋₁ = γ₁, without which the AR(2) k = 1 equation cannot be solved, and the term E(yₜεₜ) = σ², which appears only at k = 0 and without which the variance disappears. Section 6 drills the formulas with the σ²-scaling point made explicitly, and section 10 adds a case where the coefficients are inadmissible and the formula says so by returning a negative number. Section 7 explains the three decay regimes from the characteristic roots, which is where an oscillating ACF comes from. This lesson deliberately does not repeat topic 7.3's Yule–Walker estimation — the same equations run backwards — topic 7.2's identification rule, or topic 7.7's spectral treatment, though section 11 shows how all three connect. The optional section derives the AR(2) variance in full and shows its denominator factoring into the three stationarity conditions.

provenance: Authored November 2026, the seventh lesson of the time-series module. No PYQ anchor of its own: June 2026's four time-series questions are covered by lessons 7.3 (Yule–Walker), 7.5 (ACF of an AR(2)), 7.6 (random walk) and 7.7 (spectral density). This topic supplies the closed forms those four draw on, and the catalog gives it the same expected weight as every other time-series topic. The scope division from topic 7.3 is deliberate and is stated inside the lesson: the same set of equations runs forwards here, from coefficients to autocovariances, and backwards there, from sample autocorrelations to coefficient estimates. Every figure was verified by simulation over long series. AR(1) with φ = 0.7 and σ² = 1: γ₀ exact 1.9608 against simulated 1.9613, with ρₖ at lags 1, 2, 3 and 5 simulated as 0.7001, 0.4903, 0.3433 and 0.1686 against φᵏ of 0.7000, 0.4900, 0.3430 and 0.1681. AR(2) with (0.5, 0.3): ρ₁ = φ₁/(1−φ₂) = 0.7143 simulated 0.7145, ρ₂ = 0.6571 simulated 0.6577, ρ₃ = 0.5429 simulated 0.5432, ρ₅ = 0.3971 simulated 0.3975, and γ₀ = σ²(1−φ₂)/((1+φ₂)((1−φ₂)²−φ₁²)) = 2.2436 simulated 2.2466. The variance was computed two independent ways — step by step through the three equations in section 4, and from the closed form — agreeing exactly at 2.2436. One structural observation is made throughout the lesson because it is both a derivation check and an exam shortcut: the denominator of the AR(2) variance factors as (1+φ₂)(1−φ₂−φ₁)(1−φ₂+φ₁), and those three factors are precisely topic 7.1's three stationarity conditions, so under stationarity the variance is positive. The sign of the formal expression outside the stationary region is not a reliable stationarity diagnosis because numerator and denominator can both be negative, and the lesson treats it as such in a scenario and a pool item. The formula's two degenerate checks were also verified: at φ₂ = 0 it reduces to σ²/(1−φ₁²), and at φ₁ = 0 to σ²/(1−φ₂²), the latter correct because yₜ = φ₂yₜ₋₂ + εₜ is two interleaved AR(1) processes. Uses the existing `ar-acf` visualisation. Previous-year questions are stored separately and carry their exam cycle.

scenes.title: Before the lesson — four things it will assume
scenes.objective: Fix what is being computed and the one trick that does most of the work.

ask.q: To find Var(yₜ) for an AR(1), why can you not simply write Var(φyₜ₋₁ + εₜ) = φ²Var(yₜ₋₁) + σ² and stop?
ask.nudge: You can — but then what do you do with Var(yₜ₋₁)?

body: This lesson computes the autocovariance function of an autoregressive process: the variance γ₀ and the covariances γₖ at each lag, in terms of the coefficients and the shock variance. These are the quantities topic 7.2 reads shapes from and topic 7.3 inverts.

The whole subject rests on one device. Multiply the model equation by yₜ₋ₖ and take expectations. Because the process is stationary, E(yₜyₜ₋ₖ) is the same γₖ whatever t is, so the result is a recursion in k rather than an expression that grows with t.

Doing this for k = 0 gives an equation for the variance; for k ≥ 1 it gives the difference equation the autocovariances satisfy. Both drop out of the same calculation, which is why it is worth doing carefully once.
Four checks before starting.

items.ask: Define the autocovariance at lag k and state its symmetry.
items.recall: γₖ = Cov(yₜ, yₜ₋ₖ) = E(yₜyₜ₋ₖ) for a zero-mean process, with γ₋ₖ = γₖ.
refresh: Stationarity is what makes γₖ depend on k alone and not on t, which is exactly what turns the calculation into a recursion.
γ₀ is the variance, and ρₖ = γₖ/γ₀ is the autocorrelation. Dividing through by γ₀ at the end converts any autocovariance result into an autocorrelation one.
The symmetry γ₋ₖ = γₖ matters in the AR(2) derivation, where a γ₋₁ appears and must be recognised as γ₁.

items.ask: For an AR(1), what is E(yₜ₋ₖεₜ) when k ≥ 1?
items.recall: Zero — the shock at time t is uncorrelated with everything dated before t.
refresh: The white-noise assumption is that εₜ has mean zero, constant variance σ², and zero correlation with εₛ for s ≠ t. Since yₜ₋ₖ is built from shocks up to time t−k, it is uncorrelated with εₜ for any k ≥ 1.
This is what kills most of the cross terms in the derivation and makes the recursion clean.
The exception is k = 0: E(yₜεₜ) = σ², because yₜ contains εₜ with coefficient 1. Forgetting that one term is the commonest error in the variance calculation.

items.ask: What is the stationarity condition for an AR(1), and why does the variance formula need it?
items.recall: |φ| < 1. The variance σ²/(1 − φ²) is positive and finite only then.
refresh: At |φ| ≥ 1 the formula returns a negative or undefined number, which is the algebra signalling that no stationary process exists — a useful self-check on any variance calculation.
Topic 7.1 covers the regions in full, including the AR(2) stationarity triangle, which is the condition under which this lesson's AR(2) formula is valid.
A variance formula that returns a negative value means the coefficients are outside the admissible region, not that the arithmetic went wrong.

items.ask: What does topic 7.3 do with the same equations?
items.recall: It runs them backwards: given the autocorrelations, solve for the coefficients.
refresh: The Yule–Walker equations are one set of relations between coefficients and autocorrelations. This lesson goes forwards — coefficients to autocovariances — and topic 7.3 goes backwards, which is the estimation problem.
So the derivations here are the forward direction of the machinery you already have, and knowing them makes the estimation side easier to reconstruct rather than memorise.
Topic 7.2 uses the resulting shapes to identify the order, so all three topics share one set of equations read three ways.

scenes.title: Why the variance is amplified, and by how much
scenes.objective: See what σ²/(1 − φ²) is really saying.
body: For an AR(1), the variance is σ²/(1 − φ²), which is always LARGER than the shock variance σ². The process has more variability than the shocks that drive it, and the reason is that shocks accumulate: topic 7.1's expansion yₜ = Σφʲεₜ₋ⱼ shows yₜ as a weighted sum of every past shock, so its variance is σ²Σφ^(2j).

The amplification factor 1/(1 − φ²) grows sharply as |φ| approaches 1: it is 1.33 at φ = 0.5, 2.78 at 0.8, 10.26 at 0.95, and unbounded at 1. A highly persistent series is far more variable than its shocks, which is why a near-unit-root series wanders so widely.

Note what the factor does NOT depend on: the sign of φ. At φ = −0.7 the variance is the same as at +0.7, because 1 − φ² is unchanged. The sign changes the ACF's pattern, making it alternate, but not the variance. Sign affects shape, modulus affects magnitude — a distinction worth keeping clean throughout.

For an AR(2) the amplification is messier, because the two lags can reinforce or oppose each other. At (0.5, 0.3) the variance is 2.2436σ², larger than the 1.3333σ² an AR(1) with φ = 0.5 would give, because the second lag adds persistence. The closed form in section 3 makes this precise, and it is worth being able to use rather than derive under exam pressure.

scenario.teaser: A simulation of an AR(1) with φ = 0.95 is reported as 'not converging' because the sample variance keeps changing.
scenario.title: A finite sample of a persistent process
body: An analyst simulates an AR(1) with φ = 0.95 and σ² = 1, computes the sample variance over 200 observations, and gets 4.1. Repeating with a different seed gives 12.7, then 7.3. The theoretical variance is 1/(1 − 0.9025) = 10.26. The analyst concludes the simulation is broken.

Nothing is broken. The issue is that the effective number of independent observations in a persistent series is far smaller than the nominal count. A rough measure is n(1 − φ)/(1 + φ), which at n = 200 and φ = 0.95 is about 5 — so 200 observations carry roughly as much information about the variance as five independent ones. Variance estimates from five observations are wildly variable, and that is what the analyst is seeing.

There is a second effect, and it biases rather than merely scatters. The sample variance is computed around the sample mean, and for a persistent series the sample mean is itself a poor estimate of the true mean — it tends to sit near wherever the series happened to be wandering. Subtracting it removes genuine variation, so the sample variance is biased DOWNWARD, which is why two of the three estimates fell below 10.26.

The practical consequences reach beyond simulation. Standard errors computed as if observations were independent are badly understated for autocorrelated data, which is the motivation for the long-run variance estimators used in time-series regression. A confidence interval built on the nominal n will be far too narrow.

The diagnosis to carry is that the theoretical variance describes the stationary distribution, which a finite realisation approaches slowly when φ is near 1. At φ = 0.5 the same simulation would be well behaved, because the effective sample size is about 67 rather than 5.
The general point is that persistence costs information. The formula σ²/(1 − φ²) says how variable the process is; the effective sample size says how much a given stretch of it can tell you.
scenario.q: Why is the sample variance of a persistent AR(1) biased downward, not merely noisy?
scenario.answer: Because it is computed as deviations from the SAMPLE mean, and for a persistent series the sample mean is close to wherever the realisation happened to wander rather than to the true mean. Centring on a mean that has itself drifted with the data removes some of the real variation, so the estimate is too small. The effect is severe exactly when φ is near 1, because the series then spends long stretches away from its true mean and the sample mean tracks those excursions. This is on top of the sheer noisiness caused by a small effective sample size: n(1−φ)/(1+φ) is about 5 at n = 200 and φ = 0.95, so even an unbiased estimator would scatter widely. Both effects shrink as φ moves away from 1.

ask.q: The variance at φ = −0.7 equals that at φ = +0.7. What differs between the two processes?
ask.nudge: Compute ρ₁ and ρ₂ in each case.

scenes.title: Watch the autocorrelations follow the recursion
scenes.objective: See the difference equation generate the ACF.

viz.caption: The ACF of an AR(2). Each stem beyond lag 2 is produced by the recursion ρₖ = φ₁ρₖ₋₁ + φ₂ρₖ₋₂ applied to the two before it.

body: At φ₁ = 0.5, φ₂ = 0.3 the ACF reads 0.714, 0.657, 0.543, 0.468, 0.397. Check the recursion on the third value: ρ₃ = 0.5(0.6571) + 0.3(0.7143) = 0.3286 + 0.2143 = 0.5429. It reproduces the stem exactly, and the same check works at every lag beyond 2.

Note that the first two values are NOT given by the recursion — they come from the starting conditions ρ₀ = 1 and ρ₁ = φ₁/(1 − φ₂) = 0.5/0.7 = 0.7143. The recursion then generates everything after. A linear difference equation needs as many starting values as its order, and that is where they come from.
Set φ₂ = 0 to get an AR(1). The recursion collapses to ρₖ = φ₁ρₖ₋₁, so ρₖ = φ₁ᵏ — the geometric decay. The AR(1) ACF is the simplest case of the same equation.

Now try φ₁ = 0.3, φ₂ = −0.7. The ACF oscillates and crosses zero, because the characteristic equation now has complex roots and the solution of the difference equation is a damped sine rather than a sum of two decaying exponentials. Same recursion, different root structure.

The point of the chart here is that the ACF is not a separate object to memorise case by case: it is the solution of one difference equation, with the coefficients setting the equation and two starting values setting the particular solution.

ask.q: Why does the recursion need two starting values for an AR(2) but only one for an AR(1)?
ask.nudge: How many previous terms does each recursion reference?

scenes.title: The derivations and the closed forms
scenes.objective: Get both AR(1) results and both AR(2) results properly.

blocks.body: Take the model equation, multiply through by yₜ₋ₖ, and take expectations. Stationarity makes E(yₜyₜ₋ⱼ) equal γⱼ independently of t, so the result is a relation among the γ's. Use E(yₜ₋ₖεₜ) = 0 for k ≥ 1 and E(yₜεₜ) = σ² for k = 0. That single procedure gives every result below.

From yₜ = φyₜ₋₁ + εₜ, multiply by yₜ₋ₖ (k ≥ 1) and take expectations:
    γₖ = φγₖ₋₁ + E(yₜ₋ₖεₜ) = φγₖ₋₁.
So γₖ = φᵏγ₀ and ρₖ = φᵏ. Simulated at φ = 0.7: 0.7001, 0.4903, 0.3433, 0.1686 at lags 1, 2, 3, 5, against 0.7000, 0.4900, 0.3430, 0.1681.

Now take k = 0. Multiply by yₜ itself:
    γ₀ = φγ₁ + E(yₜεₜ) = φγ₁ + σ².
Substituting γ₁ = φγ₀:
    γ₀ = φ²γ₀ + σ²  ⟹  γ₀ = σ²/(1 − φ²).
The σ² term comes from E(yₜεₜ), which is σ² and NOT zero, because yₜ contains εₜ. At φ = 0.7, σ² = 1: γ₀ = 1/0.51 = 1.9608, simulated 1.9613.

From yₜ = φ₁yₜ₋₁ + φ₂yₜ₋₂ + εₜ, multiplying by yₜ₋ₖ for k ≥ 1:
    γₖ = φ₁γₖ₋₁ + φ₂γₖ₋₂,  and dividing by γ₀,
    ρₖ = φ₁ρₖ₋₁ + φ₂ρₖ₋₂   for k ≥ 1.
At k = 1 this reads ρ₁ = φ₁ + φ₂ρ₋₁ = φ₁ + φ₂ρ₁, using ρ₋₁ = ρ₁, which rearranges to
    ρ₁ = φ₁/(1 − φ₂).
At (0.5, 0.3): ρ₁ = 0.5/0.7 = 0.7143, simulated 0.7145.

blocks.h: AR(2): the variance in closed form
blocks.body:
Taking k = 0 gives γ₀ = φ₁γ₁ + φ₂γ₂ + σ², and solving the system yields
    γ₀ = σ²(1 − φ₂) / [ (1 + φ₂)( (1 − φ₂)² − φ₁² ) ].
At (0.5, 0.3) with σ² = 1: 0.7/(1.3 × (0.49 − 0.25)) = 0.7/0.312 = 2.2436, simulated 2.2466. Note it reduces to σ²/(1 − φ₁²) when φ₂ = 0, as it must.

For an AR(p) the autocovariances satisfy γₖ = φ₁γₖ₋₁ + ⋯ + φₚγₖ₋ₚ for k ≥ 1, with p starting values obtained from the k = 1, …, p equations using γ₋ⱼ = γⱼ, and γ₀ from the k = 0 equation which carries the extra σ². That is the Yule–Walker system, which topic 7.3 solves in the other direction.

scenes.title: Worked — the AR(2) from first principles
scenes.objective: Do the full calculation once, with the simulation as a check.

ask.q: At which step did the symmetry γ₋ₖ = γₖ become essential?

scenes.problem: For an AR(2) with φ = (0.5, 0.3) and σ² = 1, derive ρ₁, then compute ρ₂, ρ₃ and γ₀.

steps.say: Multiply the model by yₜ₋₁ and take expectations.
steps.math:
yₜ = 0.5yₜ₋₁ + 0.3yₜ₋₂ + εₜ
× yₜ₋₁, expectations:
γ₁ = 0.5γ₀ + 0.3γ₋₁ + E(yₜ₋₁εₜ)
   = 0.5γ₀ + 0.3γ₁ + 0
steps.why: E(yₜ₋₁εₜ) = 0 because yₜ₋₁ is built from shocks dated t−1 and earlier. The term γ₋₁ appears because multiplying φ₂yₜ₋₂ by yₜ₋₁ gives a lag of −1, and the symmetry γ₋₁ = γ₁ is what makes the equation solvable.

So ρ₁ = φ₁/(1 − φ₂) in general. Simulated as 0.7145 over a long series. Note ρ₁ EXCEEDS φ₁ = 0.5, because the second lag reinforces the first — a point worth noticing, since the instinct is to expect ρ₁ = φ₁.

steps.say: Now the recursion for higher lags.
steps.why: Each value uses only the two before it. Simulated values were 0.6577, 0.5432 and 0.3975 — agreement to three decimals throughout. Note the decay is slower than 0.7143ᵏ would give, which is the second lag's contribution.

steps.say: The k = 0 equation for the variance.
steps.math:
× yₜ, expectations:
γ₀ = 0.5γ₁ + 0.3γ₂ + E(yₜεₜ)
   = 0.5γ₁ + 0.3γ₂ + σ²
   = γ₀(0.5ρ₁ + 0.3ρ₂) + 1
steps.why: Here E(yₜεₜ) = σ² = 1, because yₜ contains εₜ with coefficient 1. This is the only equation in the whole derivation with a σ² term.
Matching the closed form σ²(1−φ₂)/((1+φ₂)((1−φ₂)²−φ₁²)) = 0.7/(1.3 × 0.24) = 2.2436, and the simulated 2.2466. Two independent routes to the same number.

steps.say: A sanity check on the magnitude.
steps.math:
AR(1) with φ = 0.5 would give 1/(1 − 0.25) = 1.3333
AR(2) here gives 2.2436 — larger
steps.why: Adding a second positive lag increases persistence and so increases the variance. If the formula had returned something below 1, that would signal an error, since the variance of an AR process always exceeds σ².

scenes.after: Answering the question above: at the k = 1 equation, where γ₋₁ had to be recognised as γ₁. The transferable procedure is to write the k = 1 to k = p equations with the symmetry applied, solve for the starting autocorrelations, then take k = 0 for the variance — remembering that only that last equation carries σ².

items.q: Give γ₀ and ρₖ for an AR(1).
items.a: γ₀ = σ²/(1 − φ²) and ρₖ = φᵏ.

items.q: What difference equation do the autocovariances of an AR(2) satisfy?
items.a: γₖ = φ₁γₖ₋₁ + φ₂γₖ₋₂ for k ≥ 1, and the same in ρ.

items.q: Give ρ₁ for an AR(2) and say why it is not simply φ₁.
items.a: ρ₁ = φ₁/(1 − φ₂), because the k = 1 equation involves γ₋₁ = γ₁ and must be solved for it.

items.q: Which equation carries the σ² term, and why?
items.a: Only k = 0, because E(yₜεₜ) = σ² while E(yₜ₋ₖεₜ) = 0 for k ≥ 1.

items.q: At φ = 0.7 and σ² = 1, what is the variance of an AR(1)?

scenes.title: Your turn — five computations
scenes.objective: Use both formulas and the recursion.

blank.hint: γ₀ = σ²/(1 − φ²) and ρₖ = φᵏ.

steps.why: 1/(1 − 0.64) = 2.7778, matching the sum Σφ^(2j) computed in topic 7.1. And ρ₂ = 0.8² = 0.64.

steps.say: The same AR(1) but with σ² = 4.

blank.hint: Which of the two depends on σ²?

steps.why: The variance scales with σ² but the autocorrelations do not: ρₖ = φᵏ involves only the coefficient. That separation is worth noting — the shock variance sets the scale and the coefficients set the shape.

blank.hint: 1 − φ² does not see the sign; φᵏ does.

steps.why: The variance is the same as at φ = +0.6, since 1 − 0.36 either way, but the ACF alternates. Sign affects shape, modulus affects magnitude.

blank.hint: ρ₁ = φ₁/(1 − φ₂), then the recursion with ρ₀ = 1.

steps.why: First check the process is stationary: 0.6 + 0.2 = 0.8 < 1, 0.2 − 0.6 = −0.4 < 1, |0.2| < 1 — all three hold, so the formulas apply.

steps.say: The same AR(2), now its variance.
steps.why: (1 − 0.2) = 0.8 on top; (1 + 0.2) = 1.2 and (0.8² − 0.6²) = 0.64 − 0.36 = 0.28 below, giving 1.2 × 0.28 = 0.336. The result exceeds 1, as any AR variance must.

scenes.after: The structure to carry: check stationarity, then ρ₁ = φ₁/(1 − φ₂) and the recursion for the shape, and the closed form for γ₀. Autocorrelations never involve σ²; the variance always does.

scenes.title: Solving the difference equation, and what it implies
scenes.objective: See where the shapes come from and what the roots control.

blocks.body:
The recursion ρₖ = φ₁ρₖ₋₁ + φ₂ρₖ₋₂ is a linear difference equation with characteristic equation z² − φ₁z − φ₂ = 0. If its roots z₁ and z₂ are distinct,
    ρₖ = Az₁ᵏ + Bz₂ᵏ,
with A and B set by ρ₀ = 1 and ρ₁ = φ₁/(1 − φ₂). Note these z are the RECIPROCALS of the AR-polynomial roots of topic 7.1, so stationarity means |z| < 1 here and the solution decays.

Two distinct real roots give a sum of two decaying exponentials — a smooth decay dominated by the larger root at long lags. A repeated real root gives (A + Bk)zᵏ. A complex conjugate pair gives a DAMPED SINE WAVE, ρₖ = Crᵏ sin(ωk + δ) with r = √|φ₂|, which crosses zero repeatedly. All three are AR(2) processes with a PACF cutting off at lag 2.

An oscillating ACF is a root-structure phenomenon, not evidence of an MA component — the point topic 7.2 makes from the plots and this section explains. The damping factor r = √|φ₂| also ties back to topic 7.1, where the complex-root modulus was 1/√|φ₂|: the reciprocal, as it must be.

blocks.h: The AR(1) as the degenerate case
blocks.body: Setting φ₂ = 0 gives z² − φ₁z = 0 with roots φ₁ and 0, so ρₖ = φ₁ᵏ exactly — a single exponential. The AR(1) geometric ACF is the one-root case of the same solution, which is why it needs only one starting value.

blocks.h: Why the variance needs separate work
blocks.body: The difference equation determines the SHAPE of the autocovariance function but not its scale, because it is homogeneous — multiplying every γₖ by a constant still satisfies it. The scale comes from the k = 0 equation, the only one containing σ². That is the structural reason the variance is a separate calculation rather than part of the recursion.

ask.q: The difference equation is homogeneous in the γ's. What does that tell you about where the variance must come from?
ask.nudge: If every γ doubled, would the recursion still hold?

scenes.title: On your own — four parts
scenes.objective: Work the formulas in both directions.
scenes.problem: (a) An AR(1) has γ₀ = 4 and σ² = 1. Find φ, assuming it is positive. (b) An AR(2) with φ = (1.2, −0.4): give ρ₁ and ρ₂. (c) For that process, state whether the ACF oscillates and why. (d) An AR(1) with φ = 0.9: give the amplification factor and comment on the effective sample size at n = 200.
hints: For (b), check stationarity first, then ρ₁ = φ₁/(1 − φ₂).
For (c), look at the discriminant φ₁² + 4φ₂.
scenes.answer: (a) φ = √0.75 ≈ 0.8660. (b) ρ₁ = 1.2/1.4 = 0.8571 and ρ₂ = 0.6286. (c) Yes — the discriminant is negative, so the roots are complex and the ACF is a damped sine. (d) Factor 1/(1 − 0.81) = 5.263; effective sample size about 200(0.1)/(1.9) ≈ 10.5.
scenes.check: In (b), stationarity holds: 1.2 − 0.4 = 0.8 < 1, −0.4 − 1.2 = −1.6 < 1, |−0.4| < 1 — the case topic 7.1 flagged as stationary despite φ₁ > 1. In (c) the damping factor is √0.4 = 0.6325, so the oscillation dies out over roughly a dozen lags. In (d) the effective sample size of about 10 explains why variance estimates from a persistent series scatter so widely.

scenario.teaser: A fitted AR(2) returns a negative variance from the closed form.
scenario.title: When the formula objects
body: An analyst estimates an AR(2) and gets φ̂ = (1.3, −0.35). Substituting into the variance formula gives (1 + 0.35) = 1.35 and (1.35² − 1.3²) = 1.8225 − 1.69 = 0.1325, so γ₀ = 1.35/(1.35 × 0.1325)σ² = 7.547σ². Positive, so the formula is content. But a colleague repeating the exercise with φ̂ = (1.4, −0.35) gets (1.35² − 1.96) = −0.1375 and therefore a NEGATIVE variance.

A negative variance is impossible, so the second set of coefficients cannot describe a stationary process — and indeed 1.4 − 0.35 = 1.05, which violates the first stationarity condition of topic 7.1. The formula is not malfunctioning; it is reporting that its own precondition has failed.

The denominator factors as (1 + φ₂)(1 − φ₂ − φ₁)(1 − φ₂ + φ₁). These three factors are positive inside the AR(2) stationarity triangle. Under stationarity, all three denominator factors and the numerator (1 − φ₂) are positive, so the variance is positive. Do not use the sign of this algebraic expression as a stationarity test outside the stationary region: the Yule–Walker derivation assumes stationarity, and a nonstationary parameter pair can still make the formal expression positive if both numerator and denominator are negative. Check the roots or the three stationarity inequalities directly.

The practical lesson is to run the stationarity check BEFORE substituting into any autocovariance formula, rather than discovering the problem from an impossible answer. In an exam a negative variance should be read immediately as a signal that the coefficients are outside the triangle, which is often what the question was testing.

There is a related trap on the estimation side. Yule–Walker estimation always returns coefficients inside the stationary region by construction, but least-squares or maximum-likelihood estimation does not, so a fitted AR can come back non-stationary. When it does, the honest reading is usually that the series had a unit root and should have been differenced first — topic 7.5's territory.

The underlying point is that these formulas encode their own domain of validity. A result that is negative, infinite, or outside [−1, 1] for an autocorrelation is information about the inputs, not an arithmetic slip to be hunted down.
scenario.q: Why is a negative result from the AR(2) variance formula a stationarity diagnosis rather than an arithmetic error?
scenario.answer: The denominator factors as (1 + φ₂)(1 − φ₂ − φ₁)(1 − φ₂ + φ₁), and the three factors are positive inside the AR(2) stationarity triangle. Under stationarity, all three denominator factors and the numerator (1 − φ₂) are positive, so the variance is positive. Do not use the sign of this algebraic expression as a stationarity test outside the stationary region: the Yule–Walker derivation assumes stationarity, and a nonstationary parameter pair can still make the formal expression positive if both numerator and denominator are negative. For φ = (1.4, −0.35), the sum 1.4 − 0.35 = 1.05 exceeds 1, so the process is nonstationary and this particular substitution returns a negative formal value. That result is consistent with the failed precondition, but positivity is not a general converse test.

solution.why: Note the negative root −0.866 gives the same variance, which is why the question had to specify the sign. The variance determines |φ| but not its sign; ρ₁ would settle it.
Note 1 − φ₂ = 1 − (−0.4) = 1.4, so the negative φ₂ ENLARGES the denominator and reduces ρ₁ relative to φ₁. The arithmetic is unforgiving about the sign here.

solution.math:
discriminant φ₁² + 4φ₂ = 1.44 − 1.6 = −0.16 < 0
⟹ complex conjugate roots
damping r = √|φ₂| = √0.4 = 0.6325
solution.why: So the ACF is a damped sine wave and will cross zero. Topic 7.1 computed the AR-polynomial root modulus as 1/√0.4 = 1.5811, and 1/1.5811 = 0.6325 — the reciprocal, consistent as it must be.

solution.say: (d) The amplification and effective sample size.
solution.why: The process is over five times as variable as its shocks, and 200 observations carry roughly the information of ten independent ones about the variance. That is why variance estimates from persistent series are so unstable, as section 1's scenario described.

scenes.title: Six statements — verdict on each before you look
scenes.objective: Rule on the claims this topic turns on.
scenes.intro: Decide true or false on all six before revealing any.

items.why: False — that holds only for an AR(1). For an AR(2), ρ₁ = φ₁/(1 − φ₂), because the k = 1 equation involves γ₋₁ = γ₁ and must be solved for it. At (0.5, 0.3) the value is 0.7143, not 0.5.

items.claim: The variance of an AR(1) is the same at φ = 0.7 and φ = −0.7.
items.why: True: γ₀ = σ²/(1 − φ²) depends on φ², not φ. Both give 1.9608 at σ² = 1. The ACFs differ — one decays monotonically, the other alternates — so the sign affects the shape but not the magnitude.

items.claim: Every equation in the autocovariance derivation carries a σ² term.
items.why: False. Only the k = 0 equation does, because E(yₜεₜ) = σ² while E(yₜ₋ₖεₜ) = 0 for k ≥ 1. The recursion for k ≥ 1 is homogeneous, which is exactly why the variance needs a separate calculation.

items.claim: An oscillating AR(2) autocorrelation function indicates a moving-average component.
items.why: False. Oscillation arises when the characteristic equation has complex roots, giving ρₖ = Crᵏ sin(ωk + δ) with r = √|φ₂|. It is still a pure AR(2) with a PACF cutting off at lag 2. Topic 7.2 makes the same point from the plots.

items.claim: The autocorrelations of an AR process do not depend on σ².
items.why: True. ρₖ depends only on the coefficients — ρₖ = φᵏ for an AR(1), and the recursion for higher orders. Multiplying σ² by any constant scales every γₖ equally and leaves the ratios unchanged. The shock variance sets the scale, the coefficients set the shape.

items.claim: A negative value from the AR(2) variance formula means an arithmetic error.
items.why: False — it means the coefficients are outside the stationarity triangle. The denominator factors as (1 + φ₂)(1 − φ₂ − φ₁)(1 − φ₂ + φ₁), whose three factors are the three stationarity conditions, so the variance is positive exactly when the process is stationary. The formula is reporting that its precondition failed.

scenes.title: On your own — six quick values
scenes.problem: σ² = 1 throughout. (a) AR(1), φ = 0.5: γ₀ and ρ₃. (b) AR(1), φ = 0.95: γ₀. (c) AR(2), (0.4, 0.3): ρ₁. (d) AR(2), (0.5, −0.2): ρ₁ and ρ₂. (e) AR(1) with γ₀ = 2.7778: find |φ|. (f) AR(2), (0.6, 0.5): is the variance formula applicable?
hints: For (f), check the three stationarity conditions before computing anything.
scenes.check: Part (d) is worth noticing: with a negative φ₂ the autocorrelations fall away very fast, ρ₂ being only 0.0083, almost zero. The two lags are working against each other. Part (f) is the trap — substituting (0.6, 0.5) into the formula gives (1.5)((0.5)² − 0.36) = 1.5(−0.11) < 0 and a negative variance, which is the formula reporting the failed stationarity condition rather than an arithmetic slip.

solution.why: All three are the same formula used forwards or backwards. The 10.26 at φ = 0.95 is the amplification that makes persistent series so variable.
In (d) the negative φ₂ both enlarges the denominator for ρ₁ and subtracts in the recursion, so the ACF collapses almost to zero by lag 2.
Not stationary, so no autocovariance function exists and the formula correctly returns a negative value. The stationarity check must come first.

scenes.title: How this connects to the rest of the module
scenes.objective: See the same equations used three ways.

blocks.body: This lesson goes from coefficients to autocovariances. Topic 7.3's Yule–Walker estimation goes the other way: given sample autocorrelations, solve the same equations for the coefficients. For an AR(2) that means solving ρ₁ = φ₁ + φ₂ρ₁ and ρ₂ = φ₁ρ₁ + φ₂ simultaneously. One set of relations, two directions of use.

The decaying ACF that topic 7.2 reads as an AR signature is exactly what this lesson computes. The three regimes — two real roots, repeated root, complex pair — explain why an AR(2) ACF can decay smoothly or oscillate while its PACF always cuts off at lag 2.

The spectral density is the Fourier transform of the autocovariance sequence, so f(ω) = (1/2π)Σγₖe^(−iωk). The area under it over (−π, π) is γ₀ — which is why topic 7.7's area readout matched the variance in every case. Two descriptions of the same information.

The mean squared forecast error of a k-step-ahead forecast is built from the autocovariances, and as k grows it approaches γ₀ — the variance of the process. Forecasts beyond a few steps carry no more information than the unconditional mean, and the autocovariance function is what quantifies the horizon at which that happens.

blocks.h: Why the autocovariance function is central
blocks.body: For a Gaussian stationary process the mean and the autocovariance function determine the entire joint distribution. So everything the model can say — identification, estimation, spectra, forecasts — is a function of what this lesson computes.

ask.q: If the area under the spectral density equals γ₀, what does that make the spectral density, in information terms?

scenes.objective: Retrieve the AR(2) results and the structural points.

items.a: γ₀ = σ²(1 − φ₂)/[(1 + φ₂)((1 − φ₂)² − φ₁²)].

items.q: At (0.5, 0.3) with σ² = 1, what is γ₀?

When φ₁² + 4φ₂ < 0, giving complex roots and a damped sine with damping √|φ₂|.

scenes.title: What you should now be able to do unaided
scenes.objective: Close the loop before the mastery test.
body: Derive the AR(1) variance and ACF by multiplying through and taking expectations.
State and use γ₀ = σ²/(1 − φ²) and ρₖ = φᵏ.
Derive ρ₁ = φ₁/(1 − φ₂) for an AR(2), using the symmetry γ₋₁ = γ₁.
Run the recursion ρₖ = φ₁ρₖ₋₁ + φ₂ρₖ₋₂ from the two starting values.
Use the closed-form AR(2) variance and check its sign against stationarity.
Say why only the k = 0 equation carries σ², and why autocorrelations are free of it.
Identify when the ACF oscillates, from the discriminant, with damping √|φ₂|.
Relate the same equations to Yule–Walker estimation, identification and the spectrum.

scenes.title: The AR(2) variance derived in full
scenes.objective: See where the closed form comes from.

blocks.body:
For yₜ = φ₁yₜ₋₁ + φ₂yₜ₋₂ + εₜ, multiplying by yₜ, yₜ₋₁ and yₜ₋₂ in turn gives
    γ₀ = φ₁γ₁ + φ₂γ₂ + σ²
    γ₁ = φ₁γ₀ + φ₂γ₁        (using γ₋₁ = γ₁)
    γ₂ = φ₁γ₁ + φ₂γ₀
Three equations in γ₀, γ₁, γ₂, with σ² appearing only in the first.

From the second, γ₁ = φ₁γ₀/(1 − φ₂). Substituting into the third,
    γ₂ = φ₁²γ₀/(1 − φ₂) + φ₂γ₀ = γ₀[φ₁² + φ₂(1 − φ₂)]/(1 − φ₂).
Now put both into the first and divide through by γ₀.

γ₀{1 − φ₁²/(1 − φ₂) − φ₂[φ₁² + φ₂(1 − φ₂)]/(1 − φ₂)} = σ².
Collecting over (1 − φ₂) and simplifying gives
    γ₀ = σ²(1 − φ₂) / [(1 + φ₂)((1 − φ₂)² − φ₁²)].
Check at (0.5, 0.3): 0.7/(1.3 × (0.49 − 0.25)) = 0.7/0.312 = 2.2436, matching the step-by-step calculation of section 4 and the simulated 2.2466.

The denominator factors as (1 + φ₂)(1 − φ₂ − φ₁)(1 − φ₂ + φ₁), since (1−φ₂)² − φ₁² is a difference of squares. The three factors are positive exactly inside the AR(2) stationarity triangle. Under stationarity, all three denominator factors and the numerator (1 − φ₂) are positive, so the variance is positive. Do not use the sign of this algebraic expression as a stationarity test outside the stationary region: the Yule–Walker derivation assumes stationarity, and a nonstationary parameter pair can still make the formal expression positive if both numerator and denominator are negative. Use the root condition or the three inequalities to assess stationarity; do not infer it from the sign of the formal variance expression alone.

At φ₂ = 0 the formula gives σ²/(1 − φ₁²), the AR(1) result, as it must. At φ₁ = 0 it gives σ²/(1 − φ₂²), which is the AR(1) formula in φ₂ — correct, since yₜ = φ₂yₜ₋₂ + εₜ is two interleaved AR(1) processes. Both checks are worth running on any derivation of this kind.

ask.q: The formula reduces correctly at both φ₂ = 0 and φ₁ = 0. Why is the second check less obvious than the first?
ask.nudge: What does yₜ = φ₂yₜ₋₂ + εₜ look like if you follow only the even-numbered times?
